**The Whispers of the Forgotten Library**

In the heart of an unnamed city, where the streets hum with the echoes of footsteps long gone, there stands a library no one remembers. Its doors, carved with symbols that shift when you aren’t looking, have not been opened in a century—or perhaps a thousand years. The windows are always dim, even at noon, as if the light itself hesitates to enter.

They say the library was built by a scholar who sought to preserve every story ever told, every dream ever dreamed. But stories, like living things, do not like to be trapped. They wiggle free from pages, slither into the corners of the shelves, and whisper to those who wander too close. Some claim to have heard voices there—soft, overlapping murmurs in languages no one recognizes. Others swear they’ve glimpsed figures in the stacks, flickering like candle flames, only to vanish when they turn.

I went there once, on a dare. The air smelled of old paper and something sweeter, like rain on stone. The first book I touched fell open to a page with my name on it—but the handwriting was my own, though I’d never written those words. The sentence read: *"You were always going to find this."* I snapped the book shut. The next one I pulled from the shelf was blank until I looked at it, then the ink bled into the paper, forming a map of a place I’d never been but somehow knew.

The librarian was a woman with silver hair and eyes the color of twilight. She didn’t ask my name. She only smiled and said, *"You’re late. The books have been waiting."* Then she vanished between the shelves, and I realized I was no longer alone. The whispers had stopped. They were all listening to me.

I left before I could find out what they wanted. But sometimes, when the wind blows just right, I hear the pages turning.

And I wonder if the library remembers me.
